questions.q: Your shop creates thousands of product objects, and every price must be a whole number of kobo. Which form of object creation fits best?
questions.explain: A factory function is one place that every product has to pass through, so the check is written once and cannot be skipped. Literals repeat the shape by hand, and Object.create(null) solves a different problem (dictionaries with outside keys).
options: An object literal written out for each product
A factory function such as createProduct(name, priceKobo) that checks the price and returns a new object
Object.fromEntries, because it is faster than a literal

questions.q: A word counter uses const counts = {} and counts[word] = (counts[word] || 0) + 1. For the word "constructor" it stores a long string instead of 1. Why?
questions.explain: Every object literal inherits names such as constructor and toString. Reading one gives the inherited function, and function + 1 is string concatenation. A dictionary made with Object.create(null), or a Map, has no inherited names.
options: Object keys cannot be English words
counts["constructor"] already exists: it is inherited from Object.prototype, so the code adds 1 to a function
|| turns every value into a string
Keys longer than 10 characters are converted to strings

questions.q: You store each user's cart in a plain object keyed by the user object: carts[ada] = […], carts[grace] = […]. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Property keys are strings or symbols. Any other key is converted to a string first, and every plain object becomes "[object Object]". A Map keeps object keys by identity.
options: Nothing: objects are valid keys and each user gets their own cart
It throws a TypeError: keys must be strings
Both users turn into the same key, "[object Object]", so the second cart replaces the first
The keys are stored as symbols and cannot be listed

questions.q: Which properties does { ...source } copy?
questions.explain: Spread copies own (not inherited) and enumerable (listed) properties. Nested objects are shared, not copied, so spread is a shallow copy. Methods on a class's prototype are inherited, so they are not copied.
options: Every property, including inherited methods and hidden ones
The source's own, enumerable properties, one level deep
Own properties only, at every level of nesting
Only properties that were created with Object.defineProperty

questions.q: An object has a getter get totalKobo() { … }. What does { ...obj } put in the copy under totalKobo?
questions.explain: Spread reads each property, which runs the getter, and stores the result as an ordinary data property. The copy's total never changes afterwards. To copy the getter itself, use Object.defineProperties({}, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(obj)).
options: The same getter, so the copy recomputes the total on each read
A plain value: the result of calling the getter once, at copy time
Nothing: getters are skipped by spread

questions.q: What is the real difference between Object.assign(target, source) and { ...target, ...source }?
questions.explain: Both copy own, enumerable properties one level deep. Object.assign assigns into its first argument, so it mutates that object and triggers any setters on it. Spread creates a fresh object.
options: There is none; Object.assign is just the older spelling
Object.assign makes a deep copy, spread a shallow one
Object.assign changes and returns the existing target (going through its setters); spread always builds a new object
Spread copies inherited properties, Object.assign does not

questions.q: After Object.defineProperty(order, "id", { value: "ORD-7" }), what are the attributes of id?
questions.explain: defineProperty sets every attribute you leave out to false. So this one line makes id read-only, hidden from Object.keys and JSON, and impossible to delete. Properties made by normal assignment get true for all three.
options: writable, enumerable and configurable are all true, like any property
writable, enumerable and configurable are all false
It depends on whether order is frozen

questions.q: What happens when code assigns to a read-only (non-writable) property?
questions.explain: Strict mode turns silent failures into errors. Modules and classes are always strict, so you see the problem at the exact line. In old scripts the assignment does nothing and your code carries on with the old value.
options: The value changes anyway; read-only is only a hint
In strict mode (all ES modules and classes) it throws a TypeError; in old non-strict scripts it is silently ignored
The property is deleted and recreated with the new value

questions.q: A teammate suggests storing a user's password hash as a non-enumerable property "so nobody can see it". What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: Enumerable controls listing, not access. user.passwordHash and Object.getOwnPropertyNames still reveal it. Keep secrets out of objects that leave your server by building the outgoing object from an allow-list.
options: Nothing: non-enumerable properties cannot be read
Non-enumerable properties are deleted when the object is copied
Non-enumerable only hides the property from listings such as Object.keys and JSON; any code can still read user.passwordHash

questions.q: You want to stop typos from creating new properties on an account, but the balance must still change. Which call fits?
questions.explain: seal fixes the shape: no new properties and no deletions, but existing values can still be changed. freeze would also stop the balance from changing.

questions.q: Which lock still allows delete obj.note but refuses obj.extra = 1?
questions.explain: preventExtensions only stops additions. seal also stops deletions, and freeze also stops changes to values.
options: None of them; they all refuse deletion

questions.q: What does Object.freeze(config) return?
questions.explain: All three locking functions change the object in place and return it, which is why const config = Object.freeze({ … }) works. Freezing cannot be undone.
options: A frozen deep copy of config; the original stays changeable

questions.q: What do you get from structuredClone(new Account("Ada")), where Account is a class with a deposit method?
questions.explain: structuredClone copies data, not behaviour. The prototype link is lost, so the methods are gone. It throws only when it meets a function stored in a property.
options: A new Account with its own copy of deposit
A DataCloneError, because class instances cannot be cloned
A plain object with the same data properties; it is not an Account and has no deposit
The same object, because class instances are copied by reference

questions.q: An order has placedAt: new Date(…) and tags: new Set(["gift"]). After JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(order)), what are they?
questions.explain: JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. A date turns into its ISO string and stays a string; a set has no enumerable properties, so it becomes {}. structuredClone keeps both.
options: A Date and a Set, exactly as before
A string and an empty object {}
A number (the timestamp) and an array

questions.q: new Set([{ sku: "RICE-5" }, { sku: "RICE-5" }]).size is 2. Why?
questions.explain: Like ===, a Set checks whether it is the same object, not whether the contents look the same. To deduplicate by content, use a key that identifies the data, such as the SKU.
options: Sets never remove duplicates of objects by accident: this is a bug in JavaScript
A Set compares objects by identity, and these are two different objects
The second object was added before the first finished
Sets compare only the first property

questions.q: Where does Object.is(a, b) give a different answer from a === b?
questions.explain: For objects both compare identity. The only differences are the two number edge cases. That makes Object.is a good default inside an equality helper.
options: Only for NaN (equal to itself) and 0 versus -0 (different)
For strings: Object.is ignores upper and lower case
Never; they are the same function

questions.q: const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user removes the hash before sending a user to the client. What is the long-term risk?
questions.explain: Removing known bad fields lets every unknown field through. For data leaving your server, list the fields that may go (an allow-list), so new fields stay private until someone decides otherwise.
options: Rest makes a deep copy, which is slow
The hash is still inside publicUser, just hidden
It is a block-list: when someone adds a new secret field to user later, it is sent automatically
Rest cannot be used with objects that came from a database

questions.q: What happens when this setter runs? set priceKobo(value) { this.priceKobo = value; }
questions.explain: this.priceKobo = value is an assignment to the very property the setter guards, so it triggers the setter again. Store the real value somewhere else: a closure variable, a #private field or a differently named property.
options: The assignment calls the same setter again, forever, until RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

questions.q: Reading report.summary runs a getter that loops over 200,000 orders and writes a log line. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Getters are not cached; each read runs them again. Keep getters cheap and free of side effects. A method call makes the cost visible to whoever calls it.
options: A property read looks cheap and harmless, so callers will read it often; expensive work or side effects belong in a method such as report.buildSummary()
There is no problem: getters are cached after the first read

questions.q: What does Object.defineProperty(obj, "vat", { value: 7.5, get() { return 7.5; } }) do?
questions.explain: A property either stores a value or runs accessor functions. Mixing the two kinds in one descriptor is refused.
options: Defines vat as 7.5 and ignores the getter
Throws a TypeError: a descriptor is either a data descriptor (value, writable) or an accessor descriptor (get, set), never both

questions.q: A price list is loaded once at start-up and only ever read by request handlers. Each handler currently calls structuredClone(priceList) before reading it. What is the better design?
questions.explain: Copying protects against changes. If nobody changes the data, sharing it is safe, and freezing it turns "nobody changes it" into a rule the engine enforces. Cloning a large object on every request wastes time and memory.
options: Keep cloning: sharing objects is always unsafe
Deep-freeze the list once and share it; a copy is only needed when someone will change the data
Seal the list so handlers can add their own prices

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Integer-like keys come first, sorted as numbers. The other string keys follow in the order they were added, not alphabetically.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The number key 1 is converted to the string "1", so both lines write the same property, and the second write wins.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Later sources win. The defaults were spread last, so they overwrote the customer's free delivery. Keys keep the position where they first appeared, which is why deliveryKobo comes first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: isVip && {…} is false, and spreading false or null in an object literal adds nothing. That is why the pattern works for optional properties.
options: TypeError: Cannot convert null to object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: count lives on Cart.prototype, so it is inherited, not own: spread skips it. The copy is a plain object, printed without the Cart label.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spread ran the getter once and stored 1200 as a plain number. But items was copied by reference, so the snapshot's array is the cart's array and now has 3 items. A snapshot that is half frozen and half live is a classic shallow-copy bug.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The example runs as a module, so strict mode is on and writing to a frozen property throws a TypeError. The value stays 7.5.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A sealed object keeps its shape (no additions, no deletions) but its values can still change. Use freeze to stop the change too.
options: change ok, add failed, delete failed 500
change failed, add failed, delete failed 1000
change ok, add ok, delete failed 500
change ok, add failed, delete ok 500

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow. config itself is frozen, but the nested deliveryKobo object is not, so its lagos value can change. Deep-freeze configuration with a recursive function.
options: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'lagos'

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: structuredClone keeps dates and maps. The JSON round trip turns the date into a string and the map into an empty object, because a map's entries are not properties.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: defineProperty made note non-enumerable (the default), so JSON and Object.keys skip it. Reading it directly still works.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The top level was copied, so changing copy.name leaves ada.name alone. The address object is shared, so changing its city changes it for both.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: b is a new object, so it is not identical to a, even with the same contents. c is another name for a. The strings inside are primitives and compare by value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: console.log does not run getters, so it shows [Getter]. JSON.stringify reads every own enumerable property, which runs the getter, so the JSON has the value.

questions.q: Finish deepFreeze(value) so it freezes an object and every object or array inside it, at any depth, and returns the value. Non-objects are returned unchanged. The program should print true true true.
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow, so the function calls itself on every own value first, then freezes the object. The isFrozen check stops it from walking the same object twice.

questions.q: Write pick(obj, ...keys): it returns a new object with only the listed keys that obj really has as own properties. Missing keys must not appear at all.
questions.explain: Object.hasOwn ignores inherited names such as toString, and Object.fromEntries builds the result from the [key, value] pairs.

questions.q: Write shallowEqual(a, b): true when both objects have the same own enumerable keys and each value is the same according to Object.is. Key order must not matter.
questions.explain: Compare the key counts first, then check each key exists on the other object with an identical value. Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself. The last case is false because the two arrays are different objects: shallow equality does not look inside them.

questions.q: Count how often each tag appears. Some tags are named after inherited properties, so the counts must be correct for them too. Print the counts with JSON.stringify.
questions.explain: {} inherits constructor and toString from Object.prototype, so the first read returns a function instead of undefined. Object.create(null) gives a dictionary with no inherited names. A Map would also work.

questions.q: Use Object.defineProperty to add an id of "ORD-7" to order. It must appear in JSON but must not be changeable. The program then tries to change it.
questions.explain: Leaving writable out makes it false, so the assignment throws in strict mode. enumerable: true must be written explicitly, or JSON would skip the id.

questions.q: Add a getter totalKobo to the cart literal that adds up priceKobo * qty for every item. It must stay correct after items are added.
questions.explain: A getter is computed on every read, so it cannot go out of date when the items change. Read it without parentheses: cart.totalKobo.

questions.q: Finish createLine(sku): the returned object has a qty accessor. The setter accepts only whole numbers from 1 to 99 and throws a RangeError otherwise; the value lives in the closure variable qty.
questions.explain: The setter checks the value before storing it in the closure variable, so a bad write leaves the old value in place. Number.isInteger rejects the string and the fraction in one check. Storing it in this.qty instead would call the setter again forever.

questions.q: Write toPublic(user) with an allow-list: it returns only id, name and city, whatever else the user object contains, without changing the user.
questions.explain: Destructure the allowed fields and build a new object from them with shorthand. Spreading the whole user leaks every field, including ones added later.
